PATTERN 01

Payer Rejects Same-Day E/M + Psychotherapy as Duplicate

Psychiatrist bills 99214 + 90833 for a combined medication management and therapy session. Payer's automated system flags the same-day combination as a duplicate charge, two services billed for one visit. Both codes denied. $110 to $182 per session permanently lost on every qualifying visit.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX submits 99214 + 90833 combinations with the documentation excerpt confirming separately identifiable E/M and psychotherapy elements. Clinical notes reviewed to confirm both services are documented distinctly before any dual-code claim is submitted. Payer-specific add-on billing rules applied per carrier.

PATTERN 02

96130–96137 Denied for Unit Count or Authorization Mismatch

Authorization obtained for 8 hours of neuropsychological testing. Actual testing completed: 6.5 hours. Claim submitted with units calculated for 8 hours. Payer denies, authorized hours don't match billed units. Or: 96138 billed for technician-administered testing that the psychologist performed, wrong code, automatic denial.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX calculates testing units from actual time documented in the psychologist's report, verifies unit count against the authorization, and applies 96130 vs 96138 based on who administered the test. Authorization-to-billing match confirmed before every testing claim.

PATTERN 03

Payer Downcodes 99232/99233 to 99231 on Hospital Claims

Psychiatrist documents complex daily note supporting 99233, high complexity MDM, medication adjustment, safety assessment, coordination with team. Payer auto-downcodes to 99231 on every admission day because the note lacks the specific complexity language their audit algorithm looks for. Systematic underpayment on every inpatient day.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX reviews inpatient notes for 99231/99232/99233 level-specific documentation language before submission. When payer downcodes a billed level, PMEX files appeal with documentation excerpt showing MDM complexity. Systematic inpatient downcoding is appealed at the pattern level, not claim by claim.

PATTERN 04

Inpatient Admission Length Denied for Insufficient Clinical Justification

Patient admitted for acute suicidal ideation. Hospitalized 7 days. Payer approves 4 days. Claims for days 5–7 denied for "medical necessity not established for continued stay." Attending psychiatrist's daily notes do not document specific clinical criteria the payer's UM criteria require for inpatient authorization.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX reviews daily inpatient notes against payer-specific medical necessity criteria (MCG, InterQual) and prompts documentation completion before concurrent review is submitted. Days 5–7 of stay supported with documented clinical justification matching the payer's UM criteria precisely.

PATTERN 05

Psychiatric NP Claims Denied, Not Enrolled with Payer

PMHNP starts seeing patients in January. Practice bills under PMHNP's own NPI. Medicare enrollment pending. BCBS rejects, provider not found in their network. Claims for February, March, and April go unprocessed until someone realizes the credentialing was never completed. Three months of revenue at risk.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX manages PMHNP credentialing with all payers simultaneously from hire date, bills under the supervising psychiatrist's NPI with correct incident-to documentation during the enrollment period, and transitions to the PMHNP's own NPI upon confirmation. No revenue gap between hire date and first independent payment.

PATTERN 06

Commercial Payer Applies Stricter Auth to Mental Health Than Medical

Payer requires prior authorization for outpatient psychiatric visits after 8 sessions. No prior auth required for comparable medical specialty visits. This MHPAEA parity violation generates systematic denials for sessions 9+ for every mental health patient with that payer, often undetected because each denial looks like an authorization issue, not a parity violation.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX monitors authorization requirements for mental health versus comparable medical services by payer. When a parity violation pattern is identified, PMEX files formal MHPAEA complaints with documentation and appeals denied claims on parity grounds. Parity violation denials recovered retroactively when pattern is confirmed.

THE EDUCATION

What Makes MHMental Health Billing in the USA Especially Complex

MH billing requires three completely different billing skill sets operating in parallel psychiatric E/M coding, psychological testing billing, and inpatient facility coding. Most billing teams specialize in at most one.

Mental health medical billing is the specialized process of submitting and managing reimbursement claims for psychiatric evaluation, medication management, psychotherapy, psychological testing, and inpatient psychiatric care to U.S. insurance payers and government programs. The billing complexity spans three distinct environments that each require different expertise, different code sets, and different documentation requirements.

The first environment is outpatient psychiatric E/M billing. Psychiatrists doing medication management visits bill E/M codes (99212 through 99215) based on medical decision-making or total time. When the same visit also includes psychotherapy, add-on codes 90833 (30 min), 90836 (45 min), or 90838 (60 min) can be billed alongside the E/M code. This combination nearly doubles the per-session reimbursement and is missed on the majority of qualifying visits in most U.S. psychiatric practices because the billing team did not read the documentation carefully enough to recognize the combined service.

The second environment is psychological testing. Neuropsychological and psychological testing requires CPT codes 96130 and 96131 for the psychologist's administration and interpretation, plus 96136 and 96137 for technician-administered testing. Prior authorization from Medicare and most commercial payers is required before testing begins. Authorization is often obtained for hours of testing but the claim is submitted incorrectly because the billing team does not know how to allocate units across the code set.

The third environment is inpatient psychiatric billing. Initial evaluation (99221-99223), subsequent care (99231-99233), and discharge (99238-99239) each have daily documentation requirements and time thresholds that differ from outpatient coding. Billing a hospital inpatient psych claim with the wrong code level or missing a daily note results in systematic denial across an entire admission.

THE BIGGEST MISSED REVENUE IN U.S PSYCHIATRIC BILLING

The Psychiatric E/M + 90833 Add-On Trap:
How U.S Psychiatrists Leave $100K to $450K Per Year on the Table Without Knowing It

When a U.S. psychiatrist provides medication management (an E/M service) and also performs psychotherapy during the same session, U.S. payer rules allow billing for both services. The E/M code (99213, 99214, 99215) covers the medical decision-making. Add-on code 90833 (30-minute psychotherapy), 90836 (45-minute), or 90838 (60-minute) covers the therapy time.

The catch: both services must be separately documented in the clinical note. The E/M portion must be significant and separately identifiable from the psychotherapy. Most psychiatrists perform both services in a combined note format which is clinically fine but creates a billing gap because the coder cannot identify the two separate elements to bill both codes.

PMEX trains on psychiatric note formats. Our specialists recognize the dual-service structure in a combined note, extract the separately billable elements, and apply the correct add-on code recovering between $98 and $162 per session that would otherwise go unbilled. For a psychiatrist seeing 20 combined sessions per week, that is $100K to $168K recovered annually from visits that already happened.

Common Questions

Mental Health Billing Answered

Everything you need to know about PMEX mental health billing services

CPT 90833 is a psychotherapy add-on code for 30 minutes of individual psychotherapy when performed on the same day as an E/M service by the same physician. CPT 90836 covers 45 minutes and 90838 covers 60 minutes. When a psychiatrist does both medication management (billable as an E/M code 99213-99215) and psychotherapy in the same session, both the E/M and the add-on code can be billed. Most psychiatrists are not billing this because their billing team either does not recognize the dual-service structure in a combined note, or is not trained to separate the two components for billing purposes. PMEX reads psychiatric notes to identify every qualifying session and applies the correct add-on code. The average value per missed add-on is $98 to $162 per session.

To bill an E/M code plus psychotherapy add-on in the same session, the clinical note must document two separately identifiable services. The E/M portion must show medical decision-making or total provider time attributable to the medical evaluation and management work. The psychotherapy portion must document the psychotherapy minutes separately and show that interactive, face-to-face psychotherapy was provided. The two elements do not need to be in separate note sections PMEX specialists are trained to identify both elements within a combined psychiatric note format and extract the separately billable components.

PMEX manages the full psychological testing billing workflow. 96130 and 96131 cover psychologist evaluation, interpretation, and feedback each requires documented psychologist face-to-face time. 96136 and 96137 cover technician-administered test administration 30 minutes per unit, with a documented list of instruments administered. Prior authorization is verified against actual planned testing hours before the battery begins. The interpretation documentation is reviewed for completeness before the claim is submitted. Common errors missing the interpretation code, incorrect unit counts, auth mismatch against actual hours are eliminated before the claim leaves the office.

CPT 99231 is subsequent hospital care requiring a problem-focused interval history and examination with straightforward medical decision-making. CPT 99232 requires an expanded problem-focused interval history and examination with moderate complexity MDM. CPT 99233 requires a detailed interval history and examination with high complexity MDM. The code level must be selected based on the documented content of the daily note not the physician's preference or a system default. PMEX reviews each inpatient note and selects the level the documentation actually supports. Most psychiatric practices billing 99231 for all days have documentation that supports 99232 or 99233 on 50 to 70% of admission days.

PMEX applies the correct telehealth modifier and place of service for each payer on every mental health telehealth claim. Medicare requires modifier 95 with POS 02 for audio-video sessions at a telehealth originating site, or POS 10 for patient-home sessions. Audio-only requires modifier FQ where covered. Commercial payers have individual telehealth coverage rules that PMEX maps and updates continuously UnitedHealthcare, Aetna, Cigna, BCBS, and all state Medicaid programs. No systematic telehealth denials from modifier or POS mismatches on any PMEX client.

PMEX manages the full spectrum of mental health billing within one engagement psychiatric E/M and add-on billing for psychiatrists and PMHNPs, time-based psychotherapy CPT coding for therapists and social workers, and psychological testing billing for psychologists. PMEX identifies carve-out behavioral health plans at eligibility verification Optum Behavioral Health, Magellan Health, and Beacon Health Options are the most common carve-out entities in the U.S. market. When a patient's mental health benefits are managed separately from their medical plan, PMEX routes the claim to the correct carve-out entity. This eliminates a denial category that most mental health practices do not recognize as having a systematic cause they see the denial, resubmit to the same wrong payer, and get denied again.

Yes. PMEX bills PHP (partial hospitalization program) using HCPCS H0035 and G0129 depending on payer, and IOP (intensive outpatient program) using H0015 and applicable procedure codes. Medical necessity documentation, prior authorization, and level-of-care criteria are verified before each PHP and IOP billing cycle. Step-down notifications to payers are managed as clinical level of care changes, preventing authorization gaps during the transition from inpatient to PHP to IOP to outpatient.

PMEX manages PMHNP billing under the provider's own NPI once credentialed, and handles the supervision documentation billing under the supervising psychiatrist's NPI during the interim credentialing period. Supervision documentation requirements vary by payer some require co-signature on the note, others accept a supervision attestation statement, others bill incident-to under Medicare. PMEX tracks each payer's requirement and applies the correct billing approach for each PMHNP on your staff while individual credentialing is processed.

PMEX audits 90 days of prior claims before transitioning, identifies the top billing gaps, and implements corrections from the first claim submitted. Full AR stabilization typically takes 60 to 90 days. PMEX tracks prior authorization requirements, session limits, and medical necessity criteria by payer for mental health versus equivalent medical services. When a payer imposes prior auth for psychiatric sessions at thresholds stricter than their comparable medical coverage, PMEX documents the parity violation and files a formal MHPAEA complaint. Many mental health practices recover retroactive reimbursement from parity complaint resolutions on claims that were denied under authorization requirements that violated the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act.
